easy.explanation: He said he would take heed to his ways so that he would not sin with his tongue.
easy.q: What did the speaker decide to guard so that he would not sin?

easy.explanation: He kept his mouth with a bridle while the wicked was before him.
easy.q: Who was before the speaker when he kept his mouth with a bridle?

easy.explanation: His heart was hot within him, and while he was musing the fire burned.
easy.q: What burned within the speaker while he was musing?

medium.explanation: Even when he held his peace, his sorrow was stirred.
medium.q: What happened to the speaker’s sorrow when he remained silent?

answers: To know how frail he was
To learn who would be king
medium.explanation: He asked this so that he might know how frail he was.
medium.q: Why did the speaker ask to know his end and the measure of his days?

medium.explanation: The image of a bridle represents restraint and careful control of speech.
medium.q: What does keeping the mouth with a bridle mean in this passage?

answers: From outward silence to inward turmoil
challenge.explanation: The speaker is silent outwardly, but inwardly his heart is hot and the fire burns.
challenge.q: What major movement takes place in these verses?

answers: His words arise from strong inner emotion
He has no concern about life
challenge.explanation: His silence intensifies his sorrow and reflection until he finally speaks.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the speaker’s silence followed by speech?

answers: The limits and frailty of human life
challenge.explanation: The speaker wants to understand the brevity and weakness of his own life.
challenge.q: What does the question about the speaker’s end seek to understand?

short_answers.question: What did the speaker place on his mouth as a symbol of self-control?
short_answers.explanation: He said, “I will keep my mouth with a bridle.”

short_answers.question: What was stirred when the speaker held his peace?
short_answers.explanation: The verse says, “my sorrow was stirred.”

short_answers.question: What did the speaker ask the LORD to make known?
short_answers.answer: His end and the measure of his days.
short_answers.explanation: He asked to know his end and the measure of his days.

paragraphs.title: The Brevity and Vanity of Human Life

easy.explanation: The LORD is said to have made the speaker’s days as an handbreadth.
easy.q: How does the speaker describe the length of human days?

easy.explanation: The verse says that every man at his best state is altogether vanity.
easy.q: How is every person described at his best state?

easy.explanation: The person heaps up riches but does not know who shall gather them.
easy.q: What does a person heap up without knowing who will gather it?

medium.explanation: The shortness of life and its vanity both show that human existence is temporary.
medium.q: What connection is made between short days and vanity?

medium.explanation: The phrase presents human activity as fleeting and ultimately empty.
medium.q: What does the phrase “vain shew” most nearly mean in context?

answers: People do not control what happens to their possessions
medium.explanation: The verse stresses that a person does not know who will eventually gather his riches.
medium.q: What does the uncertainty about who will gather the riches show?

answers: People heap up riches, but their lives are vanity
People rest, but their days grow longer
People remain silent, but become kings
challenge.explanation: People are active and accumulate wealth, yet their lives are described as vain and fleeting.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between human activity and human condition?

answers: To emphasize the temporary nature of human life
To explain how riches are stored
challenge.explanation: The repetition reinforces that human life and achievement lack permanence.
challenge.q: Why is the idea of vanity repeated in these verses?

answers: The person knows exactly who will gather them
The person does not know who will gather them
The person refuses to gather them
challenge.explanation: The verse specifically says that the person knows not who shall gather the riches.
challenge.q: What detail is easy to overlook in the description of gathering riches?

short_answers.question: What comparison is made for the length of human days?
short_answers.answer: They are compared to an handbreadth.
short_answers.explanation: The verse says, “thou hast made my days as an handbreadth.”

short_answers.question: What does every man walk in?
short_answers.explanation: The verse says, “Surely every man walketh in a vain shew.”

short_answers.question: What does a person heap up?
short_answers.explanation: The verse says, “he heapeth up riches.”

paragraphs.title: Hope in God and the Plea for Deliverance

easy.explanation: He says, “my hope is in thee,” referring to the LORD.
easy.q: In whom does the speaker place his hope?

easy.explanation: He asks, “Deliver me from all my transgressions.”
easy.q: What does the speaker ask to be delivered from?

easy.explanation: He asks, “Remove thy stroke away from me.”
easy.q: What does the speaker ask the LORD to remove from him?

answers: Human weakness leads him to depend on the LORD
His wealth leads him to trust another person
Long life causes him to stop praying
medium.explanation: After describing human frailty and vanity, he places his hope in the LORD.
medium.q: How does the speaker’s hope relate to the earlier description of human life?

answers: Because the LORD had done it
Because he did not know the LORD
medium.explanation: He remained silent because he recognized that the LORD had done it.
medium.q: Why did the speaker say, “I opened not my mouth”?

medium.explanation: The speaker asks not to become the reproach or disgrace of the foolish.
medium.q: What is “the reproach of the foolish” in this context?

answers: Hope in God, deliverance from transgressions, and removal of affliction
challenge.explanation: The speaker places his hope in God, asks for deliverance from sin, and asks for the LORD’s stroke to be removed.
challenge.q: Which combination of requests appears in this section?

answers: He is silent because he recognizes God’s action, yet he continues to plead
He is silent because he has no request
He prays only to gain wealth
challenge.explanation: Although he does not answer against God, he still brings urgent requests before Him.
challenge.q: What tension exists between the speaker’s silence and his prayer?

answers: He connects his moral condition with his suffering
He cares only about outward appearance
challenge.explanation: The order of the requests places transgression and suffering together in the speaker’s prayer.
challenge.q: What may be inferred from the speaker asking first for deliverance from transgressions and then for relief from affliction?

short_answers.question: Where does the speaker say his hope is?
short_answers.explanation: He says, “my hope is in thee.”

short_answers.question: From what does the speaker ask to be delivered?
short_answers.explanation: He asks, “Deliver me from all my transgressions.”

short_answers.question: What does the speaker say the LORD did?
short_answers.explanation: He says, “I opened not my mouth; because thou didst it.”

paragraphs.title: Suffering, Transience, and the Request for Respite

easy.explanation: The verse says that rebuke causes man’s beauty to consume away like a moth.
easy.q: What does suffering cause to be consumed like a moth?

easy.explanation: He says, “I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner.”
easy.q: How does the speaker describe himself before the LORD?

easy.explanation: He asks the LORD to spare him so that he may recover strength.
easy.q: What does the speaker ask for before he goes away and is no more?

answers: It causes human beauty to fade and shows that earthly things do not last
medium.explanation: The fading of human beauty illustrates the temporary nature of human life and possessions.
medium.q: How does suffering emphasize the theme of transience?

answers: That the speaker may regain strength
That the speaker may gather riches
That the speaker may remain silent forever
medium.explanation: The speaker asks for relief so that he may regain strength.
medium.q: What does “that I may recover strength” mean in this passage?

answers: To emphasize that his earthly life is temporary
To identify who will gather his riches
medium.explanation: The terms describe someone living temporarily rather than possessing a permanent home.
medium.q: Why does the speaker call himself a stranger and sojourner?

answers: They all express human weakness and temporary existence
They all celebrate his victory over suffering
challenge.explanation: The speaker weeps, describes himself as temporary, and asks for relief before his life ends.
challenge.q: How do the tears, the speaker’s status as a sojourner, and his request for strength fit together?

answers: The speaker shares the human condition of earlier generations
The speaker is different from all other people
The speaker is describing his ancestors’ possessions
challenge.explanation: The phrase connects his temporary condition with that of those who came before him.
challenge.q: What does “as all my fathers were” emphasize?

answers: The urgency of the request for relief
Knowledge of who will gather the riches
challenge.explanation: The speaker asks for mercy and recovery before death brings his earthly life to an end.
challenge.q: What does the ending, “before I go hence, and be no more,” emphasize?

short_answers.question: What does the speaker ask the LORD to hear?
short_answers.explanation: He says, “Hear my prayer, O LORD, and give ear unto my cry.”

short_answers.question: What does the speaker ask the LORD not to hold?
short_answers.answer: His peace at the speaker’s tears.
short_answers.explanation: He asks, “hold not thy peace at my tears.”

short_answers.question: What does the speaker ask to recover?
short_answers.explanation: He asks to be spared so that he may recover strength.
